opus-5.5.text:
I think the bar we should be aiming for is something like a "visual Turing test," but a stricter version of it. It's not enough for a generated image to look plausible at first glance. It should hold up when someone actually studies it. An expert photographer, a radiologist, or an artist should look closely and still not find the telltale signs: the inconsistent shadows, the hands with the wrong number of fingers, the text that dissolves into gibberish, the reflections that don't match the scene.

Realism alone isn't the whole story, though. I'd break the standard into a few parts.

First, physical and geometric consistency. Light should behave the way light behaves. Perspective should be coherent. Objects should have plausible structure in 3D, even though we're only producing a 2D image. Many models are very good at texture and local appearance but still struggle with global structure, and that's where the illusion breaks.

Second, controllability and faithfulness. If I describe a scene with three red cups to the left of a blue bowl, I should get exactly that. Compositional prompts, counting, and spatial relationships are still weak points. A model that produces beautiful images that ignore half of what you asked for isn't really meeting the standard.

Third, efficiency. A lot of my own interest is in making these models run on devices, on a phone, not just on a rack of GPUs in a data center. For generative models to be truly useful and widely accessible, they need to deliver high quality with far fewer denoising steps, smaller memory footprints, and low latency. Quality has to be achievable within real-world constraints.

Finally, responsibility. That means provenance, watermarking, and avoiding memorization and reproduction of training data, so that as the images become indistinguishable from reality, we still have ways to establish trust.

So in short: images that survive expert scrutiny, follow instructions precisely, run efficiently enough to be in everyone's hands, and come with the safeguards that make that power trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The response calls for realistic images and precise prompt-following, but it does not propose that models function like real cameras operated through natural-language prompts.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the standard we should hold these models to is actually a fairly old one in photography, which is that a good image should tell the truth about the scene, not just look pleasing. Right now a lot of generative models are optimized to be visually impressive, and that's fine for art, but for most real applications, whether that's on a phone camera, in content creation tools, or in simulation data for autonomous systems, the output has to be physically plausible. Lighting has to be consistent, geometry has to make sense, reflections and shadows have to agree with each other, and objects can't change identity from one frame or one viewpoint to the next.

So the bar I'd set has a few parts. First, controllability: the user, or the downstream system, should be able to specify what they want precisely and get exactly that, not something in the neighborhood. Second, consistency: the same subject should remain the same across edits, across views, across time. Third, faithfulness to the real world, which means the model has an implicit understanding of physics and 3D structure, not just texture statistics. And then, very importantly for us at Qualcomm, efficiency. If the model only runs on a rack of GPUs, it's a demo, not a product. The standard should include running on-device, at interactive speeds, within a power budget, while preserving privacy because the data never leaves the device.

And underneath all of that, I'd add a trust standard. People should be able to know whether an image was generated or edited, and the model shouldn't fabricate things it wasn't asked to fabricate. If we get controllability, consistency, physical realism, efficiency, and transparency right, then generative imaging stops being a novelty and becomes a reliable tool.

r001.rationale: The response calls for precise controllability and mentions phone cameras, but it does not propose models should function like real cameras operated through natural-language prompts.

astra-6.text: I think the standard should be more than generating an image that looks realistic. The model should understand what you’re asking for and produce something consistent with that intent. You can have a beautiful image, but if the relationships between objects are wrong, or you can’t control the details that matter to you, it hasn’t really fulfilled the task. So I would look at visual quality, consistency, and controllability together. Can you refine one part of the image while preserving the things you already like? That’s an important step toward making these models useful tools for creation.

r001.rationale: The response calls for intent-aware, controllable image generation and refinement, but does not say models should function like a real camera operated through natural-language prompts.

sol-6.1.text: I think the standard should be that you can describe what you want, and the model produces an image that faithfully reflects that intention. Making a beautiful image is only part of the problem. If you ask for three objects in a particular arrangement, the model should get the number, the relationships, and the details right. And when you want to change one thing, you should be able to change that thing while preserving the rest. So I would look at fidelity to the request, visual quality, and how much control the user has over the result.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models should turn descriptions into images that match the user’s intent, but it does not communicate the proposed real-camera analogy or say the model should function like a camera operated through natural-language prompts.
